sources.entry: NUMA Memory Policy - The normative statement of policy scopes, every mode including weighted interleave, and the cpuset intersection rule.

summary.title: NUMA Memory Policy
summary.one_liner: Linux kernel reference for how NUMA memory policies (scopes, modes including weighted interleave, flags, syscalls, and the cpuset intersection rule) decide which node pages are allocated from.
keywords: how does linux choose which numa node to allocate memory from
takeaways: Memory policy has four scopes (system default, task/process, VMA, shared), and more specific scopes override more general ones; MPOL_DEFAULT falls back to the next scope.
Four modes exist: MPOL_BIND, MPOL_PREFERRED, MPOL_INTERLEAVE, and MPOL_PREFERRED_MANY, plus MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE, which uses weights from /sys/kernel/mm/mempolicy/weighted_interleave/.
MPOL_F_STATIC_NODES and MPOL_F_RELATIVE_NODES control how a policy's nodemask is remapped when the allowed node set changes; they cannot be combined.
When cpuset and memory policy both apply, the policy's nodes are intersected with the cpuset's allowed nodes; an empty result makes the policy invalid.
summary.summary: This kernel documentation page explains what Linux memory policy is and how it differs from cpusets, which restrict memory nodes administratively. It describes the policy scopes (system default, task, VMA, and shared) with their inheritance and reference-counting rules, then covers the components of a policy: the four behavioral modes (including weighted interleave) and the optional flags that control nodemask remapping. It closes with the four memory policy system calls, the numactl command-line tool, and the rule for how policies interact with cpuset constraints.
